paras: The threatened lynching of Thomas Smith occurred at Burlingame, Osage County, Kansas, in August 1880, when townspeople threatened to lynch Smith, a Black man held for a shooting that killed Wesley Thomas and mortally wounded a saloon keeper named Baker. The sheriff took Smith away by train through a large crowd at the depot, and no attack on him was reported. Telegraph reports of the shooting ran in papers across the country, but only the Emporia News mentioned the threats of lynching.

According to the telegraph dispatch, Smith and Thomas, both described as "negroes", quarreled in front of W. M. Baker's saloon over Smith's alleged intimacy with Thomas's wife. The Emporia News called Smith "a colored man" and said he had worked for Wibley & Henson of Emporia three years earlier and was well known there.

The dispatch, dated August 23, said Smith shot Thomas through the lungs and that a second shot passed through the saloon window and struck Baker in the breast. Thomas died within minutes, and Baker was described as mortally wounded.

Smith gave a different account to A. S. Houck of Emporia, who interviewed him with the sheriff's permission. In this version Thomas had accused Smith of being too intimate with his wife, which Smith denied, and came toward him with a pistol as Smith left Baker's saloon. Smith said he shot Thomas in the stomach when Thomas refused to put up his hand, and that his revolver went off when he struck Thomas with it, wounding Smith in the hand and sending a ball through the window into Baker.

After the shooting Smith gave himself up, and for a while there were "loud threats of lynching him," with some citizens going so far as to procure a rope. When Houck's train reached Burlingame on Sunday, a "very large and excited crowd" had gathered around the depot, and Sheriff Smith of Osage County brought the prisoner aboard, manacled and handcuffed. The coverage does not say where the sheriff took him.

The Emporia News reported Baker still alive but not expected to recover. Smith claimed self-defence and expressed regret over the wounding of Baker, with whom he said he had been friendly. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial, or of Baker's fate, appears in the coverage.

The shooting spread as a short telegraph item datelined Burlingame, August 23, which ran the next day in papers from the New-York Tribune and the Washington Evening Star to the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Gold Hill Daily News. Headlines treated it as a crime of passion: "A Kansas Tragedy" in the Daily Gazette, "Fatal Affray from Jealousy" in the National Republican, and "Fatal Quarrel About a Woman" in the Gold Hill Daily News. The Wheeling Register headed it "A Dark Deed," with a deck stating that one "Colored Man" had killed another and mortally wounded "a White Man," the only headline found that gave Baker's race, while the Wheeling Intelligencer grouped it under "Wicked Western Ways."

Shorter digest versions placing the quarrel on "Sunday night" appeared in Delaware and Pennsylvania papers, and a crime-column version was still running in Minnesota and Dakota weeklies on September 2. None of the telegraph versions mentioned the arrest or the crowd. The threats of lynching appear only in the Emporia News of August 27, which rested on Houck's account, headed the story "Burlingame's Bloody Boom," and called Smith "the murderer." All of the coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report was found.

The telegraph dispatch named the dead man Wesley Thomas and the wounded man Wm. or W. M. Baker, while the Emporia News called them Bob Thomas and Logue Baker. The dispatch put the shooting on the night of August 22, "last night" from an August 23 dateline and "Sunday night" in a summary, whereas the Emporia News placed it on Saturday night, with the crowd at the depot on Sunday. The dispatch had Smith firing a deliberate second shot that hit Baker, while Smith's own version, carried only by the Emporia News, described self-defence and an accidental discharge.

bases: A crowd at Burlingame made loud threats to lynch Smith, a Black prisoner, and some procured a rope (A18); the underlying shooting between two Black men is reported by the wire (A2, A5).
Citizens in a 'very large and excited crowd' threatened to lynch Smith over the shooting and procured a rope, but Smith was taken away by the sheriff and no killing or attack is reported (A18).
The shooting is corroborated by the wire (A2, A5) and the Emporia News (A18), but the lynching threats are reported only by the Emporia News (A18).

Emporia News, 'Burlingame's Bloody Boom', reported the lynching threats without comment, called Smith 'the murderer' and also gave his self-defence claim.
